104	compression [8, 19, 35], sparse attention [15, 49, 94], etc. In con-
105	trast, VLA models remain largelyunder-exploredin the architecture
106	community. Currently, enabling VLA models on robotic platforms
107	in real-time is challenging due to their latency and energy con-
108	straints. Existing robotic platforms often fail to meet the real-time
109	requirements (50–200 Hz). For instance, a well-known VLA model,
110	PAD [26], can only execute at 2.0 Hz on a mobile Nvidia Orin
111	SoC (Fig. 2). Thus, this paper aims to enable real-time and energy-
112	efficient VLA model inference on robotic platforms.
113	Among the VLA models [5, 6, 12, 20, 26, 36, 43, 53, 54, 61, 90, 92,
114	96, 105] proposed in recent years, diffusion-based models [5, 12, 20,
115	26, 36, 53, 61, 90, 92] have emerged as a promising approach for
116	robot control. Compared to other inference paradigms, diffusion-
117	based VLA models can produce smooth motion trajectories and
118	achieve better generality among unseen environments by predicting
119	the action distribution through an iterative noise-denoising process.
120	Recent works, such as Diffusion Policy [12], UVA [36], VPP [36], and
121	Diffusion-VLA [90] demonstrate that diffusion-based approaches
122	can outperform traditional auto-regressive (AR) policies in many
123	robotic manipulation benchmarks. In this paper, we primarily focus
124	on diffusion-based VLA models.
125	Motivation.Despite their advantages, diffusion-based VLA
126	models are compute-intensive. They require tens of iterative de-
127	noising steps to generate one individual action, resulting in a higher
128	latency compared to their AR counterparts. Each denoising step
129	involves executing a deep neural network (DNN) to progressively
130	refine a noisy trajectory into a valid control signal. Our roofline anal-
131	ysis in Fig. 5 shows that existing diffusion-based VLA models are
132	compute-bound rather than memory-bound. Thus, it is important
133	to reduce the overall computation of diffusion-based VLA models.
134	To do so, our key insight is that consecutive robot observations,
135	e.g., poses and images, in robotic control loops exhibit extremely
136	high similarity, given the fact that robot control operates at a high
137	frequency. Our experiment in Fig. 7 shows that over 98% of pixels
138	between consecutive camera frames often remain unchanged due to
139	the small time interval between controls. As a result, a large portion
140	of the computation during VLA inference is redundant. Potentially,
141	we can enable orders-of-magnitude speedup for diffusion-based
142	VLA inference by exploiting this temporal redundancy.
143	Framework.To exploit this insight, we proposeDeltoris, an al-
144	gorithm–hardware co-design framework for accelerating diffusion-
145	based VLA models.Deltorisexploits the high temporal similarity
146	inherent in robotic control loops and introduces atemporal-aware
147	bit-level sparsityalgorithm that processes only the differences be-
148	tween consecutive inputs (Sec. 4). Similar to the execution of spiking
149	neural networks [98],Deltorisrepresents differential inputs in bi-
150	nary form and executes computations only on active “1” bits while
151	skipping redundant operations. Our experiment shows in Fig. 17
152	that we can achieve up to 92.9% operation reduction.
153	Although our bit sparsity algorithm significantly reduces arith-
154	metic operations, it introduces additional off-chip data traffic due to
155	the extra intermediate data loading. We show that a naive bit spar-
156	sity implementation can increase the off-chip data traffic by 1.8×.
157	We found that the VLA workloads essentially shift from compute-
158	bound to memory-bound after applying our bit-level sparsity al-
159	gorithm. To mitigate the DRAM traffic overhead, we propose a
160	technique calledspeculative inferencein Sec. 5, inspired by specula-
161	tive decoding in LLMs [50, 63]. In our approach, a lightweight VLA
162	model first speculatively predicts multiple future actions, while a
163	more accurate but compute-intensive VLA model validates these
164	predictions. To maintain robustness, no actions are actually applied
165	to the robots before being validated by the larger VLA model. In this
166	way, both model weights and intermediate data of the larger model
167	can be loaded only once when validating all predicted poses. Thus,
168	our approach amortizes data loading across multiple validation
169	steps, reducing off-chip data traffic.
170	Architecture.To fully unlock the potential ofDeltoris, we
171	design a dedicated accelerator tailored for diffusion-based VLA in-
172	ference in Sec. 6. The key contribution of our design is to eliminate
173	the workload imbalance commonly observed in bit-serial accel-
174	erators that exploit bit-level sparsity. Specifically, we employ an
175	output-stationary dataflow that shares activations across multi-
176	ple processing elements (PEs). We further introduce a novel 1D
177	systolic bit-serial PE array. Compared with prior bit-serial acceler-
178	ators, our proposed PE array largely simplifies control logic and
179	improves both performance and energy efficiency. Combined with
180	our co-designed encoding and decoding modules, our architecture
181	effectively reduces both on-chip and off-chip data movement.

35	Abstract
36	Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) enhances the factual ground-
37	ing of large language model (LLM) inference by retrieving relevant
38	information from external knowledge bases. However, its dense
39	vector retrieval introduces significant latency and energy overhead,
40	becoming the primary performance bottleneck. Although recent
41	in-storage accelerators aim to reduce data movement, they still rely
42	on host or embedded processors outside the memory, where nearly
43	70% of the total retrieval time is spent. As a result, they cannot fully
44	overcome the bandwidth limitations, leading to yet another mem-
45	ory bottleneck. To tackle these limitations, we present D-NOVA,
46	a hardware–software co-designed in-storage retrieval accelerator.
47	D-NOVA executes an inverted file (IVF)-based hierarchical retrieval
48	pipeline by deeply embedding the search functionality directly into
49	the NAND memory array. This is achieved by incorporating a new
50	distance metric, Dual-bound Tight Similarity Sensing (DTS), which
51	is specifically tailored for searching within the NAND string. In
52	addition, we introduce a lightweight contrastive adapter that maps
53	embedding vectors into a DTS–friendly domain, recovering near-
54	software recall while improving performance and energy efficiency.
55	D-NOVA is up to 41.7×faster and 71×more energy-efficient than a
56	CPU baseline, and achieves 12.13×higher throughput while being
57	up to 1.26×more energy-efficient than state-of-the-art in-storage
58	RAG accelerators, demonstrating the potential of fully in-storage
59	vector search for scalable RAG acceleration.

19	    "summary": "Alongside power, DRAM has become a major limiting factor in datacenter growth. As DRAM's cost-per-bit has plateaued over the past decade, a class of emerging memory technologies, called Long-term RAM (LtRAM), offers a path to denser and cheaper main memory. However, LtRAM has three main drawbacks: asymmetric read/write latencies, limited endurance, and coarse write granularity. In an attempt to isolate software from these drawbacks, LtRAM technologies such as Intel Optane copy an approach from flash devices and introduce a translation layer that manages wear-leveling, address remapping, and read/write caching. Prior experimental studies have found these operations add significantly to LtRAM latency. 22	Abstract
23	Alongside power, DRAM has become a major limiting factor
24	in datacenter growth. As DRAM’s cost-per-bit has plateaued
25	over the past decade, a class of emerging memory technolo-
26	gies, called Long-term RAM (LtRAM), offers a path to denser
27	and cheaper main memory.
28	However, LtRAM has three main drawbacks: asymmetric
29	read/write latencies, limited endurance, and coarse write
30	granularity. In an attempt to isolate software from these
31	drawbacks, LtRAM technologies such as Intel Optane copy
32	an approach from flash devices and introduce a translation
33	layer that manages wear-leveling, address remapping, and
34	read/write caching. Prior experimental studies have found
35	these operations add significantly to LtRAM latency.
36	Rather than making LtRAM look like DRAM, we propose
37	redesigning the hardware/software interface to offload more
38	responsibility to the operating system. This design hinges
39	on one central property, Application Read-Only Memory
40	(AROM): LtRAM pages are read-only to applications and
41	written only by the OS during page migrations. AROM is
42	enforced by leveraging copy-on-write (CoW): application
43	writes to LtRAM trigger a fault that migrates the page back
44	to DRAM before the store is applied. This invariant allows us
45	to shift LtRAM management from the on-DIMM controller
46	to the operating system, drastically simplifying the DIMM’s
47	hardware. With this approach, we aim to match the per-
48	formance of pure DRAM on read-mostly workloads while
49	delivering LtRAM’s density and cost advantages.
50	1 Introduction
51	Memory has become the dominant share of server cost. Mi-
52	crosoft Azure and Meta both report that DRAM accounts
53	for over half of total server cost [11, 16], a problem that has
54	accumulated as DRAM cost-per-bit has plateaued [12].
55	Long-term RAM (LtRAM) is a recent proposal to mitigate
56	this issue. LtRAM is a class of emerging memory technologies
57	that compete with DRAM’s read latency, but with lower per-
58	bit cost. Some examples include RRAM, PCM, FeFET, and
59	MRAM. Prior work has identified LtRAM as well-suited for
60	long-lived, read-mostly data [10]. Replacing the DRAM that
61	holds such data with LtRAM has the potential to reduce
62	DRAM footprint and overall main memory cost.
63	However, LtRAM brings its own host of challenges: read/
64	write latencies are asymmetric, endurance is limited, and
65	write granularity is coarse. Intel Optane, a discontinued
66	phase-change memory (PCM) module, is the canonical real-
67	world example of LtRAM. To minimize software-level changes,
68	Optane adopted the translation-layer pattern from flash solid
69	state drives (SSD), pushing wear-leveling, address remap-
70	ping, and read/write caching into on-DIMM hardware. This
71	hardware complexity added latency on top of the raw media
72	access time and inflated module cost, diminishing the per-
73	formance and cost advantages of the underlying technology.

134	devices scale.

136	is not constrained to any single migration policy, but the right
137	one remains open. A dirty-bit-based classifier is the simplest

139	coarse: a page that passes the threshold in one observation
140	window may be written in the next. A small online predictor
141	adapts to workload patterns from a few features (e.g., time
142	since last write, recent write frequency) at low overhead,

144	which classifications were correct. The right choice depends
145	on the workload’s diversity, the available per-page metadata

147	6.2.3 What is the best wear-leveling strategy?The to-

18	Modern LLM systems increasingly rely on knowledge-selection processes that
19	produce high-value structured priors, such as ranked evidence, graph topology,
20	multimodal alignment, and confidence signals. Yet LLM serving remains funda-
21	mentally oblivious to this rich structure: once such signals are serialized into a
22	prompt, the backend observes only a flat token sequence, forcing dense and uni-
23	form consumption of the full key-value (KV) state during decoding. We term this
24	architectural mismatch the Knowledge Selection–Runtime Consumption (KSRC)
25	gap: richer contexts enlarge the full-prompt KV footprint and decode-time mem-
26	ory traffic, increasing latency and degrading throughput even when reasoning de-
27	pends on only a small fraction of the context. To bridge the gap, we propose
28	Knowledge Access Planning(KAP), a paradigm-shifting execution abstraction
29	that elevates structured knowledge priors from passive prompt-construction hints
30	into first-class physical execution artifacts. KAP establishes a universal interme-
31	diate representation (IR)—the runtime access plan—which compiles structured
32	knowledge signals to govern physical KV access without altering logical prompt
33	semantics, model weights, or training procedures. Through this IR, KAP shifts
34	LLM serving from token-aware context consumption to plan-driven, knowledge-
35	aware runtime consumption. We instantiate KAP with GRAPHSPEC, a compiler–
36	executor realization connecting structured knowledge selection to an LLM serving
37	backend. We derive a phase-boundary model for the positive-speedup regime of
38	plan-guided execution. Across 4K–128K long-context QA workloads, GRAPH-
39	SPECmaintains answer quality comparable to full-context decoding while decou-
40	pling physical KV consumption from prompt length, reducing proposal-time KV
41	access to 5.5% of source KV state at 128K, and fundamentally shifting the scaling
42	trajectory of long-context generation.
43	1 INTRODUCTION
44	The Knowledge Selection–Runtime Consumption Gap.Modern LLM systems increasingly de-
45	pend on upstream processes that select, structure, and prioritize external knowledge. Retrieval-
46	augmented generation is a prominent instance: modern pipelines combine dense retrieval, rerank-
47	ing, and structured reasoning frameworks such as GraphRAG (Edge et al., 2024) and HippoRAG
48	(Jimenez Gutierrez et al., 2024) to rank evidence, traverse graph structure, localize supporting spans,
49	and estimate confidence (Lewis et al., 2020; Karpukhin et al., 2020). Such knowledge-selection fron-
50	tends increasingly operate as semantic planning systems, yet the LLM serving backend receives only
51	their serialized residue. Prompt serialization collapses these high-dimensional knowledge-selection
52	decisions into a one-dimensional token stream, leaving the backend oblivious to the semantic struc-
53	ture already resolved upstream.

96	6 RELATEDWORK
97	Retrieval-augmented generation and graph-guided retrieval.Retrieval-augmented generation
98	grounds LLM outputs in external knowledge by retrieving relevant passages or documents before
99	generation (Lewis et al., 2020; Guu et al., 2020). Generative retrieve-and-read systems such as
100	Fusion-in-Decoder and retrieval-enhanced language models such as RETRO integrate retrieved pas-
101	sages into generation (Izacard & Grave, 2021; Borgeaud et al., 2022). Dense retrieval methods
102	such as DPR improve open-domain retrieval by learning neural passage representations (Karpukhin

109	et al., 2020), and multi-hop retrieval extends dense selection to complex questions requiring evi-
110	dence chains (Xiong et al., 2021). Graph-based retrieval and reasoning methods build structured
111	representations over entities, documents, or events for multi-hop QA (Tu et al., 2019; Edge et al.,
112	2024; Jimenez Gutierrez et al., 2024). These works improve thefrontend knowledge selectionstage.
113	KAP is complementary: it asks how the selected knowledge should be consumed by the LLM serv-
114	ing backend once it has been retrieved.
115	RAG serving and KV-cache reuse.General LLM serving systems improve batching, scheduling,
116	offloading, and cache reuse for autoregressive generation (Yu et al., 2022; Aminabadi et al., 2022;
117	Sheng et al., 2023; Kwon et al., 2023; Zheng et al., 2024). Recent RAG-specific systems optimize
118	serving by caching or reusing intermediate states of retrieved knowledge. RAGCache caches re-
119	trieved knowledge states in a hierarchy to reduce TTFT and improve throughput (Jin et al., 2024).
120	CacheBlend fuses cached knowledge chunks even when they are not strict prefixes of the input
121	(Yao et al., 2024), and TurboRAG precomputes KV caches for document chunks to accelerate RAG
122	prefill (Lu et al., 2025). RAGO studies systematic performance optimization for different RAG
123	pipelines through a structured RAGSchema abstraction (Jiang et al., 2025). These systems reduce
124	retrieval-generation latency, especially around prefill, scheduling, and cache reuse.

237	to translate them into useful runtime access plans, and the backend’s ability to execute those plans
238	without excessive metadata, scheduling, or synchronization overhead. Future KAP instantiations
239	could realize runtime access plans through alternative sparse-access, tiered-KV, or disaggregated
240	execution mechanisms. Thus, our results establish KAP as a feasible serving paradigm and identify
241	a broader design space for future runtime knowledge-consumption systems.
242	8 CONCLUSION
243	We identified the knowledge selection–runtime consumption gap as an architectural mismatch in
244	knowledge-augmented LLM serving: knowledge-selection frontends produce high-value priors
245	about relevant knowledge, yet conventional LLM serving backends consume only the serialized
246	prompt and its full KV state. To bridge the gap, we introduced KAP, a paradigm for plan-driven
247	knowledge execution organized around a universal serving-time IR that compiles structured knowl-
248	edge priors into physical-access policies while preserving logical prompt semantics. GRAPHSPEC
249	provides a reference implementation with a Graph-RAG knowledge-selection frontend and aVLLM
250	serving backend. Our phase-boundary analysis and controlled long-context QA evaluation connect
251	knowledge selectivity, runtime consumption, and systems efficiency.

83	at similar sparsity levels. Furthermore, autoregressive decoding
84	reduces computation to inherently memory-bound skinny matrix
85	multiplications, making the realized benefit of sparsity highly de-
86	pendent on how the sparse structure is represented and scheduled
87	on GPUs. Consequently, general-purpose sparse kernels [19, 44, 73]
88	often fail to provide meaningful acceleration under moderate spar-
89	sity (30–60%)—a regime typical in LLM pruning—due to limited
90	compute intensity and nontrivial metadata overheads.
91	Recent systems such as Flash-LLM [62], SpInfer [14] address this
92	limitation by introducingload-as-sparse, compute-as-densepipelines
93	that reconstruct dense tiles for Tensor Core execution, effectively

97	trast,dynamic pruning[ 11, 16, 31, 35, 37] adaptively skips compu-
98	tation for unimportant activations at runtime, offering input-aware
99	efficiency. Unfortunately, existing dynamic pruning frameworks
100	typically restrict themselves to coarse-grained or structured activa-
101	tion masks for hardware compatibility, limiting fine-grained control
102	and failing to exploit the potential of unstructured sparsity.
103	Our key insight is that static and dynamic pruning are inherently
104	complementary. Static pruning (SP) permanently removes redun-
105	dantweights, reducing memory footprint and bandwidth cost, while
106	dynamic pruning (DP) adaptively skips redundantactivations, re-
107	ducing token-dependent computation. SP and DP act along orthog-
108	onal dimensions: SP prunes weights across rows, whereas DP skips
109	activations across columns. Their sparsity patterns therefore over-
110	lap minimally andmultiplyeffective sparsity. Our roofline-based
111	analysis (Figure 1) shows that this combined sparsity significantly
112	raises compute intensity and attainable throughput in memory-
113	bound decode workloads, offering a new efficiency frontier for LLM
114	inference (for more details, see Section 3.1).

116	tical acceleration exposessystem-level incompatibilities. Existing
117	SP and DP frameworks are not directly composable: static sparse

119	tiplication (SpMM), whereas dynamic pruning induces column-wise

18	Abstract
19	Physical AI policies require inference throughout their lifecycle, including model evaluation, cloud reinforcement learning (RL)
20	rollout, edge GPU serving, and onboard deployment. Although these settings use the same checkpoint and action semantics,
21	they often rely on separate inference programs. To provide one inference path across these settings, we buildPhyAI, an Physical
22	AI inference engine with a unified runtime. PhyAI keeps architecture-specific conditioning, solver , cache, and output logic in
23	model adapters while sharing graph execution, kernels, memory management, and parallel services. The same codebase runs
24	vision-language-action (VLA) models and world-action models (WAMs) on single or multiple GPUs across onboard, edge, and
25	cloud deployments. We used the same adapter interface to add MiniCPM-Robot on the day of its release. PhyAI achieves
26	1.40× to 4.65× speedups over the official implementations of 𝜋0, 𝜋0.5, GR00T N1.7, and MiniCPM-Robot. On Cosmos3-Nano-
27	Policy-DROID, it reduces latency from 2.46 to 1.18 s on eight H20 GPUs with CFG=2 and TP=4, a 2.08× speedup. Specialized
28	runtimes remain faster in several configurations, so our goal is one runtime with competitive latency rather than the fastest
29	result in every case. The detailed profiles also show why these models need different execution policies. On a Hopper-series
30	GPU at batch size one, the 𝜋0.5 action expert accounts for 8.8% of estimated FLOPs but 57.2% of profiled latency . At batch
31	size 32, its share falls to 13.5%, throughput reaches about 100 samples/s, and the full batch takes about 320ms. Cosmos3
32	remains generation dominated and gains only 14.3% throughput as batch size increases from 1 to 16. We further introduce
33	the control-time Roofline, which distinguishes inference-bound from environment-bound control. The measured 𝜋0.5 points

233	1 Introduction
234	Physical AI policies now span vision-language-action (VLA) models such as RT -1, RT -2,𝜋0, 𝜋0.5, and GR00T,
235	as well as world-action models (WAMs) such as Cosmos3 and DreamZero ( Brohan et al. , 2022; Zitkovich
236	et al., 2023; Black et al., 2024; Intelligence et al., 2025; Bjorck et al., 2025; Agarwal et al., 2026; Ye et al.,
237	2026b; Wang et al., 2026; Zheng et al. , 2026). The same policy may be used for offline evaluation, cloud
238	reinforcement-learning (RL) rollout, shared edge serving, and onboard deployment. These settings should
239	preserve the same preprocessing, solver , and action semantics, but they often rely on separate inference
240	programs. Each path must then be optimized and validated independently , and behavior established in
241	one setting does not automatically carry to another .
242	A common inference path is difficult to build because embodied models differ in both execution struc-
243	ture and deployment requirements. An embodied request includes observation capture, preprocessing,
244	model inference, output conversion, and action execution. A 𝜋-family VLA runs a vision-language back-
245	bone followed by an iterative action expert, whereas a Cosmos3 WAM evolves video and action states to-
246	gether . Onboard execution emphasizes single-request latency , shared edge serving must balance latency
247	against throughput, and cloud rollout uses larger batches and distributed execution. These workloads
248	require different scheduling and parallel strategies even when they share the same policy interface.
249	Existing systems cover parts of this problem. FlashRT, vla.cpp, realtime-vla, and Embodied.cpp optimize
250	selected models or devices ( Su, 2026; Nguyen et al. , 2026; Ma et al. , 2025; Xu et al. , 2026a). LeRobot
251	covers data collection, training, evaluation, and a generalized asynchronous policy-inference stack that
252	can decouple remote action prediction from robot control. It does not, however , provide the same kernel-
253	level, multi-architecture execution engine targeted by PhyAI (Cadene et al., 2026). vLLM and SGLang offer
254	mature token-oriented LLM serving (Kwon et al., 2023; Zheng et al., 2024), but their execution model does
255	not directly represent reusable multimodal conditions, iterative action solvers, evolving world latents, or
256	classifier-free-guidance branches. The missing component is an inference runtime that preserves model
257	semantics while allowing each architecture and deployment setting to choose an appropriate execution
258	policy .
259	PhyAI runtime. We build PhyAI, a unified inference runtime for embodied policies. PhyAI separates
260	model-specific logic from shared execution services. Model adapters retain conditioning, solver state,
261	reusable tensors, scheduling, and action conversion. The runtime provides graph replay , optimized ker-
262	nels, memory and cache management, quantization paths, communication, and parallel execution. This
263	separation allows the 𝜋0.5 path to reuse its single-GPU runner for data-parallel execution, while Cosmos3
264	combines tensor parallelism with classifier-free-guidance parallelism.
265	The same codebase currently runs 𝜋0, 𝜋0.5, GR00T N1.7, Cosmos3-Nano-Policy , Cosmos3-Edge, and
266	MiniCPM-Robot on devices ranging from Jetson Thor to RTX 5090, A40, H100, and multi-GPU H20 and
267	A100 servers. Local inference, distributed execution, benchmarks, and rollout workers call the same model
268	path. For cloud RL, PhyAI integrates at the RLinf inference-backend boundary ( Yu et al. , 2026a). The
269	adapter interface also allowed us to add MiniCPM-Robot on the day of its release without introducing a
270	separate runtime.
271	Control-time Roofline. Lower inference latency does not always produce a proportional improvement in
272	control rate. In a sequential loop, model inference and environment execution occur one after the other .
273	Real-time chunking instead generates the next action chunk while the current chunk is being executed
274	(Black et al. , 2026). In this setting, the relevant deadline is the next action handoff. Inference that
275	finishes before the handoff is hidden within the current execution window , while inference that finishes
276	later remains on the critical path.
277	We introduce the control-time Roofline to describe this boundary . Let 𝐿inference denote the inference
278	time and 𝐿env the time required to execute the current action and advance the environment. Under ideal
279	overlap, the slower stage determines the control period:
280	𝐿overlap = max(𝐿inference, 𝐿env) .
281	The Roofline compares the inference rate with the environment execution rate. When inference is slower ,
282	the system is inference bound and lower model latency directly improves control. When environment
283	execution is slower , the system is environment bound and further acceleration creates timing margin
284	rather than a higher ideal control rate. That margin can absorb runtime variation or support more policies
285	per GPU, a less expensive device, or a larger model.

340	accelerators may cost more than serving the same fleet from a smaller pool of datacenter GPUs, especially
341	when policy requests are intermittent and the onboard devices sit idle. A remote cloud service avoids that
342	replication, but its wide-area network path adds latency and variation to the control budget. For factory
343	fleets, a local MaaS deployment can combine shared accelerators with lower network latency than

48	Abstract
49	Current large language model (LLM) inference systems uni-
50	versally deploy ultra-large-scale models using a combination
51	of Tensor Parallelism (TP) and Pipeline Parallelism (PP). How-
52	ever, existing systems treat the model parallelism topology
53	as a static configuration that cannot be flexibly adjusted at
54	runtime. This rigid design creates a fundamental contradic-
55	tion with the dynamically changing inference workloads in
56	real-world scenarios. State-of-the-art systems lack online
57	reconfiguration capabilities and can only switch configura-
58	tions by restarting the service, resulting in several minutes of
59	service interruption, KV cache loss, and prohibitive recompu-
60	tation overhead. To address this problem, this paper presents
61	ReMP, a runtime model parallelism reconfiguration frame-
62	work that supports low downtime. ReMP achieves dynamic
63	adjustment through three key techniques: (1) decoupling
64	the model parallelism topology from runtime state to avoid
65	full service reconstruction; (2) designing a two-dimensional
66	KV cache migration mechanism to preserve reusable cache
67	states after TP/PP changes; and (3) implementing end-to-end
68	online reconfiguration. Experiments demonstrate that ReMP
69	can complete most topology switches within 1-7 seconds
70	on models ranging from 7B to 70B parameters, achieving
71	speedups of tens to over a hundred times compared to the
72	restart approach. Moreover, ReMP significantly outperforms
73	fixed configurations under dynamic workloads, delivering
74	superior performance in terms of TTFT, TPOT, and output
75	throughput.

78	1 Introduction
79	Large language model (LLM) serving systems increasingly
80	rely on model parallelism to deploy models exceeding single-
81	GPU memory capacity. In practice, inference engines com-
82	bine tensor parallelism (TP) and pipeline parallelism (PP) to
83	distribute weights, computations, and key-value (KV) caches
84	across multiple GPUs. However, existing systems treat model
85	parallel topology as a static pre-deployment configuration:
86	once launched with a given TP/PP degree, weight partition-
87	ing, KV cache layout, workers, and communication groups
88	become tightly coupled to this topology.

104	5 Conclusion
105	This paper presents ReMP, a runtime model-parallelism re-
106	configuration framework that enables adaptive LLM serving
107	without full service restart. ReMP decouples model weights,
108	KV cache, communication state, workers, and scheduler
109	metadata from a fixed TP/PP topology, and supports low-
110	downtime switching through shared-memory model reload-
111	ing, two-dimensional KV cache migration, prebuilt parallel-
112	state snapshots, and worker reuse.
113	Our evaluation shows that ReMP completes most topol-
114	ogy switches within seconds, substantially reduces recon-
115	figuration cost over restart-based switching, and improves
116	latency and throughput under dynamic request pressure.
117	ReMP demonstrates that model-parallel topology can be
118	managed as a runtime-adjustable resource for modern LLM
119	serving systems.

190	4.1 Experimental Setup
191	Hardware.
192	We evaluate ReMP on two 8-GPU platforms. The first
193	platform is equipped with 8 NVIDIA H100 GPUs, an AMD
194	EPYC 7R13 CPU, and 2TB host memory. The second platform
195	is equipped with 8 NVIDIA RTX 5090 GPUs, an Intel Xeon
196	Gold 6530 CPU, and 960GB host memory.
197	Software.We implement ReMP on top of vLLM V1. The
198	implementation adds runtime TP/PP topology switching,
199	shared-memory model state reuse, two-dimensional KV cache
200	migration, prebuilt communication-state switching, and worker
201	lifecycle management. All experiments use the same soft-
202	ware stack for ReMP and the restart-based baseline, except
203	that the baseline changes TP/PP topology by restarting the
204	serving instance.
205	Models.Table 2 summarizes the models used in our eval-
206	uation. We use four representative LLMs ranging from 7B to
207	70B parameters, including both dense and MoE architectures.
208	These models differ in parameter size, number of layers, hid-
209	den dimension, attention layout, and KV-head configuration,
210	which affect both model shard reconstruction and KV cache
211	migration during TP/PP reconfiguration.Due to GPU mem-
212	ory limitations, Llama2-70B is not evaluated on the RTX 5090
213	platform.
214	Workloads.For serving-performance experiments, we
215	use BurstGPT-derived request traces and replay them under
216	different request pressures. Each run uses the same request
217	sequence across TP/PP configurations to ensure that perfor-
218	mance differences come from the serving topology rather
219	than workload variation.
220	Baselines.For reconfiguration-cost experiments, we com-
221	pare ReMP with a restart-based baseline. The restart baseline
222	terminates the current serving instance and launches a new
223	one under the target TP/PP topology, reloading model check-
224	points, reconstructing runtime state, and discarding existing
225	KV cache.
226	For serving-performance experiments, we compare ReMP
227	with fixed TP/PP baselines. Each fixed baseline uses one
228	static TP/PP configuration throughout the workload. In con-
229	trast, ReMP uses its low-downtime switching capability to
230	probe representative TP/PP configurations under the current
231	load and then continues serving with the configuration that
232	performs best during the probing window. In the serving-
233	performance figures, we report this selected configuration
234	asReMP.
235	Metrics.For reconfiguration cost, we report restart-based
236	switching time, ReMP switching time, speedup over restart,
237	and ReMP’s internal switching-time breakdown. The break-
238	down includes model loading from the shared weight store
239	and KV cache transfer. For serving performance, we report
240	throughput and latency metrics, and compare fixed TP/PP
241	baselines against the topology selected by ReMP under each
242	model and request pressure.
243	4.2 Reconfiguration Cost
244	We first evaluate the cost of changing the TP/PP topology at
245	runtime. This experiment is designed to answer two ques-
246	tions. First, can ReMP complete model-parallel topology
247	switching within seconds? Second, how much faster is ReMP
248	compared with the conventional restart-based reconfigura-
249	tion approach?
250	For each model and topology transition, we compare ReMP
251	with a restart-based baseline. The restart-based baseline ter-
252	minates the current serving instance and launches a new
253	instance under the target TP/PP topology. This path reloads
254	model checkpoints, reconstructs worker processes, rebuilds
255	runtime and communication states, and discards the existing
256	KV cache. In contrast, ReMP keeps the serving runtime alive
257	and performs topology switching through in-memory state
258	transformation. Specifically, ReMP reuses worker processes,
259	applies prebuilt MPU-state snapshots, reloads target model
260	shards from the CPU shared-memory weight store, and con-
261	structs or migrates KV cache state according to the target
262	topology.
263	4.2.1 End-to-end Reconfiguration Time.Figures 5 re-
264	ports the end-to-end switching time of ReMP across differ-
265	ent source and target TP/PP topologies. Each cell represents
266	one topology transition, where the row denotes the source
267	topology and the column denotes the target topology. The
268	diagonal entries are omitted because they correspond to un-
269	changed configurations. The results show that ReMP can
270	complete most topology transitions within only a few sec-
271	onds.
272	On the H100 platform, ReMP completes Llama2-7B topol-
273	ogy switching in roughly 1–2 seconds across the tested transi-
274	tions. For larger models, the switching time increases because
275	more parameter shards need to be materialized under the
276	target topology, but the total cost remains low. Qwen3-30B-
277	A3B and DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-32B complete switching
278	in around 2–3 seconds for most transitions. Even for Llama2-
279	70B, whose model-shard reconstruction cost is substantially
280	higher, ReMP still completes runtime topology switching
281	within several seconds rather than requiring a full service
282	restart. We exclude transitions among 4-GPU topologies for
283	Llama2-70B, because these configurations cannot provide
284	sufficient GPU memory for valid serving runs.
285	The RTX 5090 platform shows a similar trend.
